source.title: CHIRP: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Open-Ended Response Evaluation in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Alexis Roger; Prateek Humane; Daniel Z. Kaplan; Kshitij Gupta; Qi Sun; George Adamopoulos; J. Lim; Quentin Anthony; E. Fennell; Irina Rish

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates scaling-related results in a vision-language model suite, reporting training-loss plots and associations between training loss, model scale, and benchmark performance. It does not reproduce the original language-model loss-scaling or compute-optimal allocation methods.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own Robin VLM loss-scaling plots and its own downstream benchmark results and loss-performance associations. Claims about scaling laws from cited prior work are not results of this study. Numeric loss values in Figures 7–8 are not present in the supplied text, so they are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study is mainly a benchmark paper, and the Robin scaling suite serves as its test bed. It still reports its own results on how 20 VLMs (Pythia LLM × CLIP encoder) change with component size. These cover downstream scores on existing benchmarks and on CHIRP, the link between CHIRP Elo and final training loss, and log-log plots of training loss against size. That is a new setting (VLM instruction tuning) bearing on V6 and, weakly, V5. No power law is fitted, no held-out loss is reported, and nothing is extrapolated or compute-allocated.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that existing VLM benchmarks miss differences, including scaling trends, that open-ended long-form evaluation via CHIRP reveals. They find CHIRP performance correlates with training loss more than other tasks do, and that AI judges (especially GPT-4V R) can serve as a reasonable proxy for humans despite low case-level agreement (kappa ≤ .216).
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a multimodal Robin suite with controlled LLM and vision-encoder size variations and reports final training loss and downstream evaluations. It does not use held-out language-model pretraining loss, fit the original scaling-law equations, extrapolate from small runs, or optimize parameter-token allocation under fixed compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Observed outcome varies with evaluator and criterion: human evaluations show a monotonic vision-encoder-size trend, while AI evaluations do not generally do so; GPT-4V (R) and LLaVA-34B also differ in their reported vision-encoder trends.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors suggest an ideal encoder-to-LLM size ratio. Large encoders with the smallest LLM, and large LLMs with the smallest encoder, are dispreferred by humans (Sec 6.3, App C.2.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In composite multimodal models, the size balance between components affects downstream quality, separately from total parameters.

record.problems: The reported loss values and scaling curves are only shown in figures and are not numerically available in the supplied text. The loss is an average of the last 10 training iterations, not held-out loss. The suite is a limited set of VLM sizes, and the reported scaling-loss discussion does not provide fitted exponents or a quantitative test of power-law form. Human CHIRP Elo trends are described as high variance.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported results relevant to the listed versions were omitted. Individual benchmark scores across all 20 Robin models in Appendix A.4 were not expanded into separate rows; the paper's explicit aggregate trend statements are recorded in r7–r8.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute. All LLMs are pretrained Pythia checkpoints and are not retrained.
No fit is made on small runs and extrapolated to larger ones.
No compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens.
No depth or width comparison at a fixed parameter count.
No fitted power-law form or exponents. No held-out loss. No image-only or video models, repeated data, or transfer.
Gives no predictive law and does not use pretraining loss; only association measures (dCor, % agreement) and qualitative size trends.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: How often each evaluator preferred the larger model. LLM-size ablation: human 68.5%, LLaVA-34B 66.5%, GPT-4V(S) 76.5%, GPT-4V(R) 79.4%. Encoder-size ablation: 61.3%, 53.0%, 65.2%, 66.4%.

Per-model scores on six existing benchmarks for all 20 models. The text-extracted row order of this rotated table is ambiguous (possibly reversed), so the direction of the size trend needs checking against the PDF.
OCRBench and MathVista for all 20 models. OCRBench rises from ~0–1% at 410M to ~6–17% at larger LLMs, non-monotonically. MathVista stays flat at ~17–23%.
Long-form response accuracy is more sensitive to parameter count. On 100-question GQA/TextVQA samples, only weak scaling trends appear under all grading methods.
Human overall-preference graph: overwhelming preference for larger models, reversed for the ViT-B / Pythia-410M models.

record.verdict_notes: This is a benchmark paper; scaling evidence is incidental, and the Robin suite is a test bed. Loss is mean training loss over the final 10 steps of VLM training (LoRA finetuning of the LLM), not held-out pretraining loss. The LLMs are off-the-shelf Pythia checkpoints, so scale varies only in components. The CHIRP-based rows (r5, r6, r9–r11) use the authors' own benchmark, but they do measure downstream performance vs scale and loss, so they are kept. Text extraction of Table 5 is unreliable for row order.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss of language models as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute budget is allocated between parameters and tokens, and no compute-optimal parameter or token trends are estimated.
The study varies LLM and vision-encoder sizes, but does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.

Tests a VLM setting and reports training-loss scaling plots, not held-out loss or a fitted power law. Does not test image-only or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning loss scaling as a separate regime, or transfer.

Reports benchmark and CHIRP performance trends and associations with final training loss for its Robin VLM suite; does not test downstream predictability from held-out pretraining loss or establish a general predictive law.
Does not compare fitting choices, estimate exponents, test parameter-counting or training-schedule sensitivity, or assess whether fitted curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: Robin scaling suite
rows.size_stated: 20 VLMs; five Pythia LLM sizes (410M, 1.4B, 2.8B, 6.9B, 12B) paired with four CLIP vision encoders (Base, Large, Huge, gigantic)
rows.stage_stated: Pretraining and finetuning; loss averaged over the last 10 training iterations
rows.operation_detail: Varied LLM and vision-encoder size and plotted training loss against total parameter count and component size.

conditions.value: total parameter count; LLM size; vision-encoder size

rows.note: The supplied text gives plot captions but not the plotted loss values or a textual conclusion that the plotted relationships follow a power law.
rows.check: Figure-only (Figs 7–8). The loss is the mean training loss over the last 10 training steps, not held-out loss. The text never states that the curves follow a power law.

rows.subject: Robin scaling suite

rows.measure: Training-loss relationship to parameter count and vision-encoder size
rows.value: The text says alignment between loss and parameter count is lower for the larger Pythia 6.9B and 12B models, and that losses for different vision encoders at a given LLM size are rather grouped.
rows.note: The authors describe weaker loss-parameter alignment at larger sizes; no fitted exponents or numerical loss values are supplied in the text.
rows.check: The source sentence in C.2.6 is garbled. It says loss decorrelates from parameter count for the 6.9B/12B models and that losses across encoders are grouped at a given LLM size. The authors offer this to explain the lower agreement in Table 16. It is a qualitative departure from clean size scaling, not a fitted result.

relationships.condition: CHIRP Elo vs final training loss, all 20 Robin models
relationships.reason: Elo is strongly associated with training loss: dCor 0.91 (human) and 0.96 (GPT-4V R) (r5, r6). The loss is training loss, not held-out loss.
relationships.display_finding: Elo has strong associations with final training loss, with distance correlations of 0.91 for human evaluation and 0.96 for GPT-4V R evaluation.

relationships.condition: CHIRP evaluations across the LLM-size ablation (ViT-g)
relationships.reason: All evaluators rank larger LLMs best across all criteria, with the largest gain from 410M to 1.4B (r9). Human Elo rises monotonically with encoder size (r10).
relationships.display_finding: All evaluators rank larger language models higher across criteria, with the largest gain from 410M to 1.4B, while human Elo also increases monotonically with encoder size.

relationships.condition: Existing benchmarks across LLM size; AI judges across encoder size; pairwise lower-loss preference
relationships.reason: There is only a slight LLM-size trend on standard benchmarks (r8). AI judges largely do not track encoder size (r11). Lower-loss models win only 60.8% and 71.2% of matchups (r3, r4). Predictability depends on the benchmark and the judge.
relationships.display_finding: Standard benchmarks showed only a slight language-model size trend, AI judges largely failed to track encoder size, and lower-loss models won only 60.8% and 71.2% of matchups.

relationships.condition: Existing benchmarks (ScienceQA, GQA, VQAv2, TextVQA, MM-Vet, LLaVA-Bench) across vision-encoder size
relationships.reason: The authors state there is no discernible relationship between encoder size and performance on any of these benchmarks (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Performance showed no discernible relationship with encoder size on any of the tested benchmarks.

relationships.condition: Robin VLM training loss vs parameter count
relationships.reason: The text reports loss decoupling from parameter count at the 6.9B/12B LLMs and grouped losses across encoder sizes (r2). There is no fitted law, and the plotted values are figure-only (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Loss decoupled from parameter count at 6.9B and 12B language models and grouped across encoder sizes, without a fitted scaling law.
